item.title: When Relationship Peace Requires Self-Betrayal
item.description:
Relationships

When Relationship Peace Requires Self-Betrayal

How to reclaim your sense of self in difficult relationships.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Relationship skills cannot compensate for another person’s inability to tolerate differences.
  • Patterns over time can reveal more about a relationship than any single conflict.
  • Boundaries guide your own behavior; they cannot control how another person responds.
  • Thoughtful distance can sometimes preserve both connection and a stronger sense of self.
Source: Mikhail Nilov / Pexels

Carol was a social worker who had spent years studying relationships. She understood boundaries, healthy communication, trauma, and emotional regulation. But there was one relationship where all her expertise seemed to fall short: her relationship with her mother.

Whenever Carol said no to something, her mother got angry or pulled away. If Carol tried to explain that something had hurt her, her mother became defensive, and in the end, Carol was the one who had to apologize. Eventually, Carol realized the best way to keep the relationship going was to hold back certain opinions, give in to her mother's wishes, and steer clear of anything that could upset her.

On the surface, the relationship looked peaceful, but the calm came at a price: Carol had to give up parts of herself to maintain it. Over time, she began to wonder: Was keeping the relationship worth losing herself?

Healthy relationships require many skills: clear communication, setting boundaries, taking responsibility for your actions, being aware of your triggers, and offering emotional support, among others.

If you work on these behaviors, they are useful tools for most relationships. But there is something we don’t talk about enough: You can do a great deal of work on yourself and yet have a relationship that doesn't function very well. This is because relationships involve more than one person. It is always important to work on your part, but it doesn’t necessarily change the other person or their part if they aren’t willing or able to change.

In Bowen family systems theory, differentiation of self is the capacity to maintain one’s thinking and principles while remaining emotionally connected to important people. The goal isn’t to become unaffected by other people, because that is impossible. It’s to become better able to observe what is happening and choose our response rather than react automatically.

For Carol, this would look like no longer trying to find the best way to explain herself to finally win her mother's understanding, or giving in just to not upset her mom. Instead, she can learn to manage herself around her mother's disapproval without immediately giving up her own position.

Look at the Pattern

Pay attention to whether you are the common factor in many relationships that go sour. When similar patterns crop up in my clients’ friendships, work relationships, and family life, it’s a sign to look more deeply at their behaviors.

However, suppose that with most people you are able to keep stable relationships in which disagreements can occur, apologies are given, misunderstandings are resolved, and the relationship moves on—yet with one individual, every disagreement turns into a crisis. What if that person also has a past filled with conflict or estrangement in other relationships?

That, by itself, gives you information that this might be a relationship that requires betraying yourself to maintain harmony.

Objectivity comes from focusing on the pattern, then deciding how to respond without assuming the only way forward is to keep the peace.

Compassion Doesn’t Require Unlimited Access

For Carol, it became especially difficult to set limits with her mom because she understood why she behaved as she did.

Like Carol, you might be aware of their childhood or the trauma they've experienced, and it's possible that they have difficulties with a mental illness, anger, emotional control, or with their own limitations; having that understanding can lead to compassion.

But compassion and access are not the same thing.

You can see why a person becomes angry without having to be available to be yelled at. You can understand someone's fear of being abandoned without letting that fear influence all of your decisions.

I’ve seen people—and even myself—get so preoccupied with trying to understand another person’s suffering that we lose sight of how the relationship affects us.

Understanding someone may change how much anger you carry toward them, which can help you manage and heal from that anger. But it doesn’t necessarily change how much contact is allowed.

Boundaries Don’t Guarantee a Good Response

A common misconception about boundaries is that once they're set properly, other people will eventually respect them. Perhaps so, but setting boundaries isn't a way to get someone else to change their behavior.

The other person is still free to dislike your boundary; they can criticize you, misinterpret your intentions, become distant, or even cut you off. Part of differentiation is stretching your capacity to tolerate another person’s displeasure—even when every instinct tells you to smooth things over just to make the anxiety disappear.

Many people believe the answer is complete cut-off; however, a wide range exists between complete closeness and complete cut-off. Maybe visits become shorter. Maybe you stop discussing certain subjects. Maybe you stop trying to convince someone to understand you. You could maintain warmth while sharing less personal information.

In some cases, when a relationship is abusive, threatening, or continuously destructive, it may be necessary to maintain a great distance or have no contact at all.

The key question is whether your decisions come from reactivity or from thoughtful reflection. If you’re facing a relationship that seems to require you to lose yourself to keep the peace, consider asking yourself:

What will occur when I cease to play my normal role? And what will happen if I stop overexplaining, rescuing, pursuing, or appeasing?

Can this person accept the idea of a separate self? Can I disagree with them and yet remain connected?

How far can I go in this relationship without losing myself?

And perhaps most importantly: What would I choose if I weren’t making this decision from guilt, fear, anger, or the need to make the other person understand? This is a question I still return to, both in my work and in my own relationships.

Remember, a person can wound others even if they are wounded themselves. You can show compassion for someone's limitations while still not being okay with how they express them. You can look at your own behavior without taking responsibility for theirs.

The challenge isn’t always finding the perfect words to make someone else understand your needs. Sometimes, the real work is getting clear about who you want to be in the relationship—even if the other person never truly understands you. In the end, your clarity about yourself is what matters most.

item.title: How to Identify an Emotionally Abusive Family
item.description:
Emotional Abuse

How to Identify an Emotionally Abusive Family

Do you have an emotionally abusive family?

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • The hostility in emotionally abusive families causes children to feel frightened, insecure and off-balance.
  • In these households, children may be bombarded with conflict, criticism, competition and chaos.
  • Denial, scapegoating, and gaslighting are often features of emotionally abusive families.

Family is supposed to be an environment where children receive the love, guidance, encouragement and support they need in order to mature into healthy adults. Unfortunately, in some families, not only are children deprived of the support and encouragement they need, but they are constantly bombarded with experiences of conflict, criticism, competition and chaos. These are what I call emotionally abusive families. The tension and hostility that exist in such families cause children to feel insecure, frightened, and off-balance.

In many households, emotionally abusive behavior ends up saturating the family environment until it seems normal. Behavior such as constant putdowns (often in front of others), unreasonable expectations, dismissing or mocking one another’s opinions, and character assassinations go on constantly. While not every emotionally abusive family looks the same, in this post, I will describe many of the common features.

Emotionally abusive families can have the following features:

  • Denial. Parents who are being emotionally mistreated by their partner deny they are being abused. They make up excuses for their partner’s behavior: “He’s going through a rough time at work right now.” “That’s the alcohol talking, that’s not how he really feels.” Abusive spouses deny they are mistreating their partner: “I don’t criticize you all the time, you’re just too sensitive.” Parents deny they are being abusive toward their children. “Oh, stop crying. I didn’t mean it the way you heard it.” “I’m having a bad day, just stay away from me.” And parents deny they are damaging their children, either when they abuse them or when they neglect them. “Don’t make such a big deal out of this. I didn’t hurt you that much.” “I’m sorry that I’m so tired all the time. But you’re a big girl, you can take care of yourself.” Children in these families also deny there is abuse going on—whether it is toward a parent, a sibling or toward themselves. “My parents argue but I wouldn’t call it abuse.”
  • There is often a sense of competition with each sibling vying for the attention and approval of their parents. Sibling bullying is rampant, often progressing into sibling abuse. The most typical scenario is that an older sibling who either witnesses abuse between their parents or experiences abuse firsthand takes their anger and feelings of frustration and helplessness out on their younger or weaker siblings. They may criticize their younger sibling relentlessly, bully or make fun of them, or they may become physically or even sexually violent toward them.
  • Parents, as well as other family members, regularly gaslight the children, telling them that what they see, hear and feel is not real. This makes it extremely difficult for children to trust their own perceptions and sense of reality.
  • Children suffer from a painful sense of aloneness and isolation. Instead of offering a sense of connectedness, in an emotionally abusive family, each person typically has to fend for themselves. There is usually no one to look to for support, no one to trust.
  • There is often a code of silence with no one talking about the abuse that is going on, especially to those outside the family. If one family member does speak up, that person is often viewed as the enemy for betraying the family and exposing the family secrets.

In an emotionally abusive family, everyone is affected. And everyone generally reacts to and participates in the family dysfunction in some way. Every family member is either being abused directly, being a witness to abuse, denying or pretending the abuse isn’t occurring, or passing the abuse along to a weaker or younger person in the family. Here are some of the ways family members react to the abuse:

  • They turn a blind eye. It can become so painful for loved ones to witness one parent abusing another, or a parent abusing a sibling that they try to block it out of their mind.
  • They become “silent partners.” This most often occurs when a parent stands by while one or more children are being abused by the other parent.
  • They minimize and normalize what is happening. Family members are good at telling themselves that what is happening is normal or is “no big deal.”
  • Blame-shifting. Blaming someone else for their poor behavior or for their problems is very common. In fact, this, combined with never taking responsibility for their mistakes, faults or shortcomings characterizes emotionally abusive behavior.
  • They blame the victim. This is a particularly common phenomenon. It occurs because it is very difficult for family members to process the reality of abuse. Instead, it is easier to convince themselves that the victim must have done something to bring on the abuse.
  • Scapegoating. Parents will often single out one child that they identify as the “problem child,” bullying them, making them feel like they don’t belong, even blaming them for all the family problems. Other children in the family will follow their parents’ lead and treat the scapegoat in the same way.
  • They take sides and often follow in the abuser’s footsteps. It is extremely common for witnesses to take the side of and identify with one parent over the other. This may be because they feel closer to either the victim or the abuser or because they are afraid of the abuser.
  • Neglect. Emotional abuse and neglect go hand in hand. An emotionally abused mother may become so worn down by her partner’s abuse that she is too tired or depressed to tend to her children. She may sleep most of the time, or, as a way of coping, she may begin to drink too much or take drugs.

If you recognize your family in the behaviors above, the first step to healing is to admit this to yourself, whether you are an adult child of such a family or you are a parent caught up in an abusive dynamic. In the coming months, I will take a deep dive into the phenomenon of emotionally abusive families based on my new book, Adult Children of Emotionally Abusive Families.

item.title: The Case for Halloween
item.description:
Child Development

The Case for Halloween

Less stress, more connection, and surprising health benefits with Halloween.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Routine casual interactions with neighbors reduce feelings of isolation and loneliness and increase belonging.
  • There are physical and mental health benefits to the act of giving.
  • Halloween provides developmental opportunities by encouraging make-believe and stimulating imagination.
Halloween offers a number of surprising benefits for childhood development and neighborhood cohesion.
Source: Mike Jones / Pexels

We are moving rapidly into the holiday season. You can’t escape the signs. Stores are selling Halloween decorations, and (way too soon!) winter holiday decorations are sharing the shelves. As a mental health professional, holidays fascinate me. Holidays are intended for us to take a break from work so that we can reunite with family and celebrate traditions. That’s not always how it goes down, though. Our big holidays require a lot of logistics and work and, at times, management of complex family dynamics, and can get very expensive—in short, they can come with a lot of stress.

Halloween, on the other hand, despite not being a day off of work, comes with little stress and expectation, and unless you have to buy three rounds of Halloween candy because you keep eating it too early (not that I have any personal experience…), it’s not terribly expensive. Of interest, minus the candy, Halloween is potentially the holiday with the most mental health benefits.

Let’s talk about the surprising benefits of Halloween.

Establishes bonds with neighbors and community

There is no other holiday that gets you and your neighbors together like Halloween. Whether you are outside decorating your houses, walking around in the fresh air to trick-or-treat at each other's houses, or having a community get-together, Halloween creates involvement in your neighborhood, strengthening neighbor bonds. Is this important? Heck, yeah. Your neighbors are some of the most important people in your lives. Routine casual interactions with neighbors reduce feelings of isolation and loneliness and increase a sense of belonging, provide social and other tangible support, and, when you are able to help a neighbor, feelings of self-worth and value.

It is a true giving holiday

Halloween is truly a giving holiday. It is the only day of the year when you welcome friends, family, and strangers alike to your door. Some communities are so good at this that people who don’t live there show up to trick-or-treat. On no other day of the year is this true. And happily for you, there are physical and mental health benefits to the act of giving. Specifically, the act of giving has been associated with decreased heart rate, blood pressure, and mean arterial pressure; decreased cortisol levels (stress hormone); stimulation of neurochemicals associated with pleasure; mood and social connection (serotonin, dopamine, and oxytocin); and decreased depression, anxiety, and loneliness. Routine giving has even been shown to increase longevity. And Halloween provides a chance to give directly to others, so if you are handing out treats, be ready for everyone. Have some no-sugar treats, dog treats, and a couple of extra trick-or-treat bags for that inevitable child who doesn’t have one. And if you are that full-sized candy bar house, please send me your address.

Halloween stimulates imagination, creativity, and social skills in children

Halloween provides developmental opportunities by encouraging make-believe and stimulating imagination through selection of their alter ego for the night, creating costumes, and decorating. Pretend play in particular has been linked to the ability to self-regulate, because it draws on attention, working memory, adaptability, and impulse control, and creativity is associated with better visual processing and verbal short-term memory and working memory. Additionally, Halloween facilitates structured social interactions with a significant number of people, copious practice of social etiquette and manners (please and thank you!), and sharing behavior (or possibly intense negotiations with siblings over the best stuff). These types of experiences throughout childhood are pivotal to cognitive, social, and emotional development, and, thus, from a developmental perspective, Halloween should be considered an action-packed opportunity.

It’s an easy holiday

Halloween doesn’t involve travel, copious amounts of time, and logistics to buy presents for, feed, and house the entire family, and, as holidays go, can be done fairly inexpensively. Halloween has a fascinating history, but over time has evolved into what we see today: a fun holiday when we can pretend to be someone or something else, scare each other in the name of fun, and of course indulge a little.

So—keep it appropriate, embrace your creativity, have some fun, enjoy the developmental benefits for your kids, don’t forget the dog, get outside, breathe the fresh air, talk to your neighbors, and enjoy the holiday with the least stress.

item.title: A Manifesto for Letting Kids Be Kids to Enjoy Wild Free Play
item.description:
Child Development

A Manifesto for Letting Kids Be Kids to Enjoy Wild Free Play

Peter Gray wants children to have more independence and less anxiety.

Posted September 15, 2026

Key points
  • Anthropologists have observed that youngsters play at the skills critical for well-being in their own culture.
  • The fundamental task of childhood is to grow ever more independent of adult care and protection.
  • A new book documents possible beneficial effects of screen time as it provides new ways for children to play.
A young student learning to use a play bow, a common play invitation signal in dogs and other animals, to get me to play with her.
Source: Marc Bekoff.

For a long as I can remember, I loved to play and wound up studying play in various animals for decades, something I still do. When I first learned of Peter Gray's work on childhood development with a focus on play, I immediately became a huge fan. He and I have published on a number of similar topics, and among the ones on which we converged, often unknowingly, was the importance of play for youngsters of many species. One example is the importance of the Golden Rule for maintaining a friendly and fair play space.1, 2

For these and many other reasons, I was thrilled to learn about Gray's highly acclaimed, paradigm-changing new book Restoring Childhood: How to Set Kids Free in the Age of Anxiety.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Restoring Childhood?

Peter Gray: In early 2024, I was gearing up to write a different book, which would be entitled Play Makes Us Human. That book would be about the role of play in shaping us through our three histories: our evolutionary history, our cultural history, and our individual developmental history. Then, in March of that year, Jonathan Haidt’s book, The Anxious Generation, was published.

While I, of course, liked the portion of Haidt’s book aimed at promoting more traditional outdoor freedom and play for children, I was concerned about the portion to which most readers were attending—the portion claiming that modern technology, especially smartphones and social media, was a major cause of the mental health decline among teens beginning around the year 2010. I had been following carefully the research on effects of such technology on teens and could see that Haidt’s book referred only to a very small set of the hundreds of relevant studies and completely ignored the many published reviews and meta-analyses of those studies, which consistently revealed no meaningful relationship between teens’ uses of such technology and their mental health. The book was feeding into what was already something of a moral panic about teens and technology, and I felt a need to bring data and reason to the public concern about this.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

PG: I am an evolutionary psychologist. Among the most powerful of the drives aimed at enabling independence is the drive to play. Anthropologists who have studied children in cultures where children have ample time and freedom to play report that children there play at the full range of skills that are crucial for human well-being everywhere and also play at the skills that they can see as critical for well-being in the culture where they are developing.

Source: Penguin Random House/with permission.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

PG: I hope to reach everyone. A message presented most forcefully in the last chapter is that all adults should feel obliged to help create a society conducive to healthy child development. I describe especially the roles of educators, parents, city and town planners, recreation departments, librarians, and pediatricians, but I conclude by asking everyone to think about what they can do to help bring more play and freedom to children’s lives.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

PG: To address this question, I will list the major insights conveyed in the book:

  • The fundamental task of childhood is to grow ever more independent of parental (or other adult) care and protection. Current societal practices are hindering, even preventing, children from pursuing that task. This has led to psychological suffering.
  • Children need time and space to play, explore, daydream, and find themselves. We are keeping children way too busy with adult-directed activities.
  • Children need less forced instruction, less oversight, more trust. All those extra hours of schooling along narrow, curriculum-determined lines are burning kids out, not educating them. Academic instruction to little kids, in preschool and kindergarten, has proven to be especially harmful.
  • Children gain courage, agency, social skills, emotional control, and much more through their independent play with other children, away from adult intervention and control. For a satisfying life, these skills are far more important than what is taught in school.
  • We need to stop forcing anxiety-inducing competitions onto children, in school and elsewhere. We should encourage cooperation, not competition. Making friends is much more important, for long-term happiness and the benefit of society, than winning.
  • We must stop thinking of childhood as a period of résumé building for some future charted by adults and start thinking of it as a period of finding oneself and figuring out how that self fits best into today’s world.
  • The parental practices that have come to be labeled “intensive parenting” are harmful to children and parents alike.
  • Teenagers need more acceptance into the culture as the apprentice adults they truly, biologically are. We need to stop treating them like infants.
  • We need to welcome kids into public spaces rather than discourage them.
  • To adapt well in today’s world, children need freedom to play and explore in digital space, just as they need freedom to play and explore in other spaces. The digital world is increasingly an integral part of all aspects of the “real world” in which our children are growing. There is no going back. The popular view that digital activities are more harmful than helpful to children and teens is not supported by science.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

PG: There is no other book like it. Historians (especially Howard Chudacoff and Steven Mintz) have written about the decline of U.S. children’s freedom to play since about 1960, but nobody has documented, to the extent that I have, the consequence of this decline on children’s well-being.

Also, my book is the first to document the beneficial effects that the computer revolution had on children’s well-being, as it provided new ways for children to play and interact with one another.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about the critical importance of "having a proper childhood" for normal development and later life, they will do all they can do to allow kids to be kids?

PG: This book is meant to be a call to action, not just an intellectually interesting exploration of the societal conditions required for healthy child development. At the end, I ask readers to go to my personal website and leave a message stating what they are doing, or gearing up to do, to help “restore childhood.” So, yes, I am hopeful.
